still_true: Wegovy's brand list price is still $1,349 a month. Almost nobody pays it, and now Novo's own authorised generic sells for a fraction of it.
Retatrutide still lists at $1,499 a month and has no TrumpRx cash price.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.
The 503B exclusion finalised in February 2027 still bars compounded copies of semaglutide and tirzepatide, and the 503A injunction stands.
Indiana's and Arkansas's 1115 waivers still require ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered and a quarterly verified weigh-in. Two misses end coverage for 12 months.

population.note: FICTIONAL. Arithmetic: current users = 11.9% × ~268M adults ≈ 31.9M. Ever-users = 20.5% ≈ 54.9M, so 8.6% (≈23.0M) have used and are off now. Restarters among current users ≈ 5.8 pts (49% of current; restarting is cheap with $49–69 generic semaglutide and the twice-yearly 90-day cessation courses). Add ≈2.0 pts of off-now users who restarted and stopped again: (5.8 + 2.0)/20.5 = 38% cycled. That is down from 40% because 4.0 pts (~10.7M) of new starters in 2029–30 dilute the share. It fits ~40% one-year persistence and ~45% restart within a year. Age-weighted check (adult shares ≈ 20/33/23/24%): 1.0 + 3.6 + 4.6 + 2.6 ≈ 11.9. 65+ recovered from 8% to 11% (≈7.0M) under the generic-first Medicare model and the 'strength-protected' marketing, though still below its 2026 peak. Income thirds average (14.5 + 12 + 9.2)/3 = 11.9. The bottom third rose the most (6.5 → 9.2) through Medicaid, the mandatory Medicaid coverage of cessation drugs, and $49 cash generics. The gradient now runs mostly through which drug people take and whether they get bone monitoring and strength coaching, more than through whether they take one at all. Off-drug population: ~23M stopped, plus ~213M never used. The never-users are mostly uninsured, younger, or in the self-described 'unmedicated' minority, which polls put at ~6% of adults who have actively declined a prescription offer. Pediatric: ~0.5% of ~73M under-18s ≈ 365k, mostly adolescents on generic semaglutide, much of it Medicaid-paid under EPSDT. No child has more than ~7 years of exposure, and adolescent bone-accrual data are still absent.

access.public_coverage: The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge expired in Dec 2029. The CMS Innovation Center 'Medicare Metabolic Health Model' (2030–2034) replaced it: generic semaglutide at a $10 copay, branded tirzepatide and retatrutide at $50 copay with prior authorisation, same BMI/comorbidity criteria, plus a required DEXA and strength-counselling visit for 65+ every 12 months. Medicare pays for 26% of incretin fills ≈ 8.3M users (≈7.0M aged 65+ plus ≈1.3M disabled under-65), of whom ≈3.8M use the drug for obesity. Obesity spend at the end-2030 run rate: 2.1M generic × $45 net × 12 ≈ $1.1B, plus 1.7M brand × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.0B, ≈ $6.1B/yr. Diabetes Part D spend falls as semaglutide goes generic. Medicaid pays for 18% of fills ≈ 5.7M users. About 2.4M of all users have cessation as a listed indication, and Medicaid must cover FDA-approved cessation drugs under ACA §2502, so every state now covers semaglutide for smokers regardless of its obesity-drug policy. Medicaid spend: 4.0M generic × $40 × 12 ≈ $1.9B, plus 1.7M brand × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.0B, ≈ $6.9B/yr, of which ≈65% (≈$4.5B) is federal. Public programmes together pay 44% of fills (≈14.0M users), more than commercial plans (35%). For adults 65+ and the poor, a public programme is now the default payer.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 60+ brands at $8–45 a month. Canada: generic semaglutide CAD 70–100. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and China all have generics. Oral generic semaglutide is sold in ~170 countries. US generic tirzepatide is not expected before ~2036.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Mechanism: in Aug 2029 Novo Nordisk settled its Paragraph IV litigation, licensing generic semaglutide entry (injectable and oral) from 1 Apr 2030 and launching its own authorised generic. By Q4 2030 three ANDA holders plus the authorised generic sell at $49–69 a month cash at Costco, Cost Plus and TrumpRx. Prices by product: Zepbound vials stay at $299–349 cash; Lilly cut Foundayo to $99 to compete with generic oral semaglutide; retatrutide lists at $1,499 with commercial net ≈$700. Payer mix of 31.9M users: commercial 35% (11.2M), Medicare 26% (8.3M), Medicaid 18% (5.7M), cash 19% (6.1M), gray/imported 2% (0.6M) = 100%. Commercial users fell slightly even though employer coverage rose from 58% to 63%: many insured people now pay $49 cash for generic so their refills stay out of PBM adherence dashboards. ~45% of covering employers run adherence gating. The ACA preventive-services rule (USPSTF 'A' rating for tobacco cessation) obliges most private plans to cover two 90-day quit attempts a year with no cost-sharing, which payers call 'the smoker's loophole'. Indian mail-order volume roughly halved after US generics launched.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic and US generics since Apr 2030)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus, and generic oral semaglutide)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist, weekly injectable (survodutide, approved Jan 2029)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: MASH / liver (semaglutide; survodutide label includes MASH data)
adjunct to cigarette smoking cessation (semaglutide, Apr 2029)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: vaping and nicotine-pouch cessation (label covers cigarettes only), widely prescribed via quitlines and telehealth
'metabolic health'/longevity low-dose use, now mostly generic oral at $49–59
microdosed 'maintenance' regimens and scheduled drug holidays, often self-titrated with cheap generic pens
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
gambling and compulsive-shopping craving reduction, still anecdotal
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. Survodutide was approved Jan 2029 (filed Oct 2027) with modest uptake. Amycretin was approved Jul 2029 (NDA Jun 2028). MariTide (monthly) is still in phase 3 and unfiled. Muscle-preserving combination: bimagrumab was in phase 2 at the start of this window, so the rules keep it off the US market through 2030. Lilly ran a 48-week phase 3 of bimagrumab + tirzepatide. Topline (Sep 2030) showed the lean share of weight lost falling from ~35% to ~12%, with no fracture endpoint. The BLA was filed Dec 2030 with a priority review voucher, and a decision is due mid-2031. The driver is realised by the filing and by an existing product in a new form: 'Zepbound Strong' is tirzepatide co-marketed with an FDA De Novo-cleared prescription digital therapeutic for resistance training and protein. Advertising describes it as 'muscle-protected', which the label does not support. Gray-market SARMs (enobosarm-type) are sold alongside generic pens. The incretin market is ≈$98B in 2030, down from $105B: volume growth is outweighed by the semaglutide generic price collapse.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common effect and the leading cause of stopping. Repeated re-escalation after drug holidays brings back nausea.
Elevated with rapid loss. Cycling users repeat the rapid-loss phase.
No causal confirmation; absolute risk low.

Unchanged: ~1.5× sarcopenia criteria in 65+ users on therapy >2 years; lean share of loss ~25–40%. 'Muscle-protected' marketing has not changed the population data, and bimagrumab data cover lean mass, not function or fractures.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label (2028) retained. The Medicare Metabolic Health Model requires an annual DEXA and strength-counselling visit for 65+. FDA sent an untitled letter over 'muscle-protected' promotional claims (2030).

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Hazard ratio still ~1.3–1.4 in 65+ long-term users, concentrated in women and in cycling users. No new data either way. Cessation coverage built around two 90-day courses a year adds a cycling pattern.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class labelling and DEXA recommendation retained. The Senate HELP report (2029) faulted Novo's disclosure. The DOJ civil matter was settled.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention; unchanged.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association, including in the smoker trial population.

Interim retatrutide postmarketing data on the anhedonia scale are inconclusive. Surveys still find ~10–15% of long-term users report reduced pleasure, dose-dependent. The term is now common but the measurement has not changed.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None beyond the postmarketing scale. The cessation label notes 'changes in reward-related behaviour' without classifying them as an adverse event.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Substantial regain within a year. Involuntary stops now come from waiver lockouts and 90-day cessation course limits rather than price.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Indiana waiver litigation continues at the 7th Circuit.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D and protein signals persist in older and high-loss users.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects (>5 years), adolescent decades-long exposure, repeated cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About eight years of follow-up exist. Adolescent bone-accrual studies are enrolling but have not reported.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements; pediatric bone-accrual studies under way.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Imported-pen poison-centre calls fell after US generics launched, but counterfeit 'generic' pens and gray SARMs sold with them persist.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion retained; import alerts; FDA warning letters to SARM sellers.

food_and_beverage.state: With ~31.9M users, up ~22%, and most new users in the bottom and middle thirds, volume pressure has reached the core value segments: dollar-store snacks, two-litre soda and large-format confectionery. Protein, fibre and bone claims are standard. A small 'full-fat, unmedicated' premium niche (butter, sourdough, whole milk) is growing in Boise, Austin and Brooklyn.

alcohol.state: Heavy-drinker volumes keep contracting. Spirits and beer majors cut forecasts again. Cigarette volume decline accelerated from ~6%/yr to ~9%/yr after the cessation approval. Convenience-store tobacco revenue in high-Medicaid states such as Kentucky and West Virginia is falling, and tobacco companies push nicotine pouches, which the label does not cover.

restaurants.state: Traffic holds. Small plates and protein-forward menus are standard, while 'full-plate' supper clubs and steakhouses market themselves to the unmedicated. Value-volume chains in high-uptake low-income suburbs now underperform as well.

apparel.state: Wider size runs per style continue. Plus-size retail is stable because of cycling regain. A soft-silhouette 'unmedicated' aesthetic sells in small independent labels.

fitness.state: Growing. The Medicare model's annual DEXA and strength-counselling visit feeds MA 'strength benefits', and DEXA-plus-coaching chains franchise into rural strip malls. Digital resistance-training therapeutics are bundled with Zepbound Strong.

insurance.state: Commercial pharmacy trend falls from ~+9% to ~+3% as semaglutide goes generic, and employer coverage rises to 63%. Cost control has become behaviour control: adherence gating, BMI surcharges up to the 30% wellness cap, and steering to generic-first formularies. Payers lobby the Preventive Services Task Force to narrow the cessation coverage that the ACA preventive-services rule extends to semaglutide.

pharma.state: Novo's US incretin revenue roughly halves under generic entry, and it relies on authorised-generic volume and ex-US sales. Lilly keeps growing on tirzepatide, retatrutide and Foundayo, and its bimagrumab filing is the sector's main story. Generic makers (Viatris-, Teva- and Indian-linked ANDA holders) gain. Total incretin sales ≈$98B.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: With a $49 generic, being thin no longer signals money. Muscle does: a DEXA report and visible strength read as 'well-managed', while being thin without muscle reads as 'generic-thin'. Visible fullness has become a declared identity, 'unmedicated', worn with a certain pride, alongside the older readings of lapsed coverage or a failed weigh-in.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The top third (14.5%) uses branded tirzepatide or retatrutide with coaching and bone monitoring. The bottom third (9.2%) uses generic semaglutide through Medicaid or cash, often the cessation indication, with less monitoring. The unmedicated identity has two class poles. One is affluent: homesteading and whole-food families in Boise's Treasure Valley, the people who can afford to opt out. The other is rural and religious and suspicious of 'medicated appetite'.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are smaller and protein comes first. Drug-holiday feasts are a new ritual: the skipped dose before Thanksgiving, a wedding or a quinceañera is planned the way people used to plan a cheat day. Unmedicated supper clubs serve bread and butter as a statement.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Profiles state 'on', 'off', 'holiday' or 'unmedicated'. Unmedicated-only dating circles exist in Boise and Austin. Couples negotiate dose-holiday weekends together.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is still treated as something to manage medically, but managing it now includes scheduled release, the deliberate weekend of wanting things. For the unmedicated, unmanaged appetite is a moral and aesthetic claim of authenticity.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Measured prevalence has not changed: surveys still find ~10–15% of long-term users report reduced pleasure, dose-dependent, and interim postmarketing anhedonia data are inconclusive. The complaint has become ordinary. 'The flats' is common slang, and a 2029 national poll found ~4 in 10 current users had deliberately skipped or lowered a dose 'to feel things'. Drug holidays are invisible to adherence gating because PDC counts pharmacy fills, not injections. Users refill on time and skip doses, and unused pens collect in refrigerators.
interior_life.framing: Called a side effect by users, 'reward modulation' by clinicians, and a treatment on the cessation label. Wellness vendors dropped the 'even-keel' pitch after it became a punchline. HR still rewards the observable correlates, but no longer names them.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Off-dose Fridays and pre-weekend skips are common in sales, hospitality and creative work. Logistics and DOT-screened drivers stay on, since sleep-apnea recertification depends on it. Some managers informally ask 'are you on holiday this week?' after a mood swing, and union contracts now bar the question.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Off-dose' albums and stand-up specials are a marketing tag. An unmedicated music and craft scene in Boise and Austin trades on fullness and excess as aesthetics. Bars run 'holiday hour' promotions on weekends.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples schedule dose holidays around anniversaries and conception attempts. Sex therapists routinely ask about dose and holiday timing. Mismatched holiday schedules are a named source of conflict.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The unmedicated movement is a cross-partisan coalition. Medical-freedom conservatives extended vaccine-status anti-discrimination laws to incretins: Montana's 2030 amendment bars employers from conditioning employment on incretin status or adherence data, though ERISA preemption limits its reach to fully insured and public plans. Fat-acceptance and disability-left groups fight the Medicaid weigh-in waivers. Commentators argue about whether a population with flattened cravings votes differently, and there is still no evidence either way.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and pro-generic. FDA expedited the final ANDA approvals once the settlement set an entry date, approved the cessation indication, and processed survodutide and amycretin on schedule. It is defensive on muscle and bone claims (untitled letter on 'muscle-protected' advertising) and still selective on imports.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The Medicare Metabolic Health Model is generic-first ($10 generic, $50 brand). Medicaid cessation coverage is mandatory under ACA §2502, and obesity coverage is optional by state, now in 31 states. The ACA preventive-services rule covers two 90-day cessation courses a year in private plans with no cost-sharing.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Expanded. Following a CMS template, Ohio, Georgia, Missouri, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Utah and Iowa adopted Indiana-style 1115 waivers: ≥80% PDC plus a quarterly kiosk weigh-in, with a 12-month lockout after two misses. That makes nine states. The cessation-indication coverage cannot legally be gated this way, which creates a two-track system within the same state. The Medicare model conditions the brand tier on the annual DEXA and counselling visit. About 45% of covering employers run PBM adherence gating, and BMI surcharges of up to 30% of premium remain legal federally. Montana restricts them for fully insured and state plans.
state.workforce_or_military: The de facto DOT sleep-apnea pathway persists for commercial drivers. The Army allows generic semaglutide for recruits under waiver, and accession data are reviewed. No mandate.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: US generics shrank the India mail-order irritant, and trade talks moved on to API sourcing, since most generic semaglutide API comes from Indian and Chinese plants. Section 232 tariffs now hit generic makers, keeping US generics at ~$49–69 rather than Indian prices of $8–45.

events.event: FDA approves semaglutide as an adjunct to cigarette smoking cessation. Because Medicaid must cover cessation drugs under ACA §2502 and the ACA preventive-services rule requires cost-free cessation courses, every state Medicaid programme and most private plans must now cover it for smokers.

Novo Nordisk settles Paragraph IV litigation with generic filers, licensing US generic semaglutide entry on 1 April 2030 and announcing its own authorised generic. Analysts cite its lost share to Lilly and the post-scandal political pressure.

CMS replaces the expiring GLP-1 Bridge with a five-year Medicare Metabolic Health Model ($10 generic, $50 brand, annual DEXA and strength counselling required for 65+) and issues a Medicaid waiver template. Seven more states adopt Indiana-style adherence and weigh-in gating.

Generic semaglutide launches in US pharmacies at $89–119. By October, with three ANDA holders and Novo's authorised generic competing, Costco and Cost Plus list it at $49–69 a month, and Indian mail-order volume falls by roughly half.

Montana amends its 2021 medical-status anti-discrimination law to bar employers from conditioning hiring, pay or premiums on incretin use or adherence data. It is backed by an unusual coalition of medical-freedom Republicans, 'unmedicated' organisers and SEIU, and its reach is limited by ERISA preemption.

Lilly reports phase 3 data showing bimagrumab plus tirzepatide cuts the lean share of weight lost from ~35% to ~12%, with no fracture data. It launches 'Zepbound Strong', tirzepatide co-marketed with a cleared digital strength therapeutic, as 'muscle-protected', and files the combination BLA in December.

open_tensions: The drug now costs $49, but the gating built to control its cost remains. Nine Medicaid waivers and ~45% of covering employers still meter adherence and weigh-ins. PDC cannot see drug holidays, Montana-style laws cannot reach self-funded plans, and the justification has shifted from cost to behaviour without anyone saying so.

The smoker's loophole: cost-free twice-yearly 90-day cessation courses have become a back door to coverage. Payers want the Preventive Services Task Force to narrow it. Meanwhile the course structure builds on/off cycling into coverage design, even though the bone ledger says cycling compounds loss.
'Muscle-protected' is being sold to Medicare-age users before the bimagrumab BLA is decided and without fracture endpoints. The annual DEXA requirement measures the problem but does not solve it.

Now that the drug is cheap, not taking it reads as a choice. The unmedicated movement has made that choice an identity, while ~213M never-users, most of them simply uninsured or young, are increasingly assumed to be opting out. Adolescents on generics are accruing exposure that no one has measured.

prose.headline: The Fifty-Dollar Shot: America's Weight Drug Went Generic. Now Everyone Wants a Day Off From It
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 about one American adult in eight is on an incretin drug, almost thirty-two million people. The drug most of them take now costs about as much as a tank of gas. In August 2029 Novo Nordisk settled its patent fights rather than wait out the clock. Its share had already gone to Lilly and its reputation to a bone-data scandal. Generic semaglutide reached pharmacies in April. By autumn three generic makers and Novo's own authorised version were competing, and Costco listed a month's supply for forty-nine dollars. Wegovy's brand list price is still $1,349, a number that now exists mainly on paper.

The price fell, and the payer changed. Medicare's temporary Bridge expired and was replaced by a five-year Metabolic Health Model with a ten-dollar generic copay and a required annual bone scan for anyone over sixty-five. Medicaid's change came through a side door. In April 2029 the FDA approved semaglutide to help smokers quit. Federal law already required Medicaid to cover cessation drugs, and it required private plans to cover two ninety-day quit attempts a year at no cost. Overnight, every state covered the drug for smokers. Public programmes now pay for more fills than employers do. In eastern Kentucky, cigarette sales at gas stations are falling faster than anyone at the tobacco companies' investor days predicted.

Cheapness did not end the monitoring. Seven more states copied Indiana's rule: refill on time, step on a pharmacy kiosk scale every quarter, or lose coverage for a year. Nearly half of employers that cover the drug still meter refills through their benefits managers. The original reason for watching was cost, and that reason is gone. The watching continues and is now described as engagement. Some insured workers now pay the forty-nine dollars themselves, so their refills never appear on a dashboard.

The quieting effect, the 'Ozempic personality' of four years ago, has become an ordinary complaint, mostly called 'the flats'. The research has not moved: about one long-term user in eight reports less pleasure, more at higher doses. But almost half of users say they have skipped a dose on purpose to feel something. Drug holidays are planned like vacations, before a wedding, a tour or an anniversary. Refill systems count pharmacy fills, not injections, so the skipping is invisible. Refrigerators across the country hold unused pens next to the butter.

There is now a visible minority who refuse. Calling yourself 'unmedicated' means soft faces, sourdough, whole milk and supper clubs where the bread is the point. In Boise and in Austin it has its own dating circles and its own bands. It also has politics. In June, Montana extended its vaccine-status anti-discrimination law to bar employers from conditioning jobs or premiums on incretin use. Medical-freedom Republicans, fat-acceptance activists and a hospital workers' union backed it together. Federal benefits law limits how far that reaches.

At the top of the market, Lilly says it has solved the frailty problem. Its muscle-preserving antibody, combined with tirzepatide, cut the share of lost weight that came from muscle by two-thirds in a trial that measured lean mass but not fractures. The combination is filed, not approved. In the meantime 'Zepbound Strong', the old drug packaged with a strength-training app, is advertised as muscle-protected, and the FDA has objected in writing. The bone warnings on the label have not changed.

Snack and soda makers that depended on value shoppers are now losing volume in their core markets. Gyms that sell a bone scan and a coach have reached rural strip malls. Thinness has stopped signalling money. Muscle signals it now, along with the discipline and coaching that produce a good DEXA report.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Lashonda Mills checks the butter shelf before her shift. There are three generic pens there, all unused, each from a refill she picked up on schedule. The Indiana Medicaid letter on the fridge says ADHERENCE IN GOOD STANDING. She is not taking this Saturday's dose either, because Brianna's quinceañera is Sunday and she wants to taste the cake.

At six she drives to her first client in Merrillville, Mr. Dobrowski, who lifts a two-pound dumbbell while she counts. His Medicare plan sends a coach on a tablet. He says the tablet is meaner than she is.

At noon she stops at the Walgreens on Broadway for her quarterly weigh-in. She puts in her shoes and her card, and the kiosk takes her picture and says VERIFIED. A woman behind her has been locked out, she tells the pharmacist, because she missed two refills when her car died. The pharmacist hands her a printout of the cash price, forty-nine dollars. The woman folds it into a very small square.

Lashonda hasn't smoked in fourteen months. The pens first came to her on the quitting prescription, two free rounds a year, before the weight one took over. Some afternoons she misses the cigarettes the way she misses being hungry, more as something that used to be hers than as a craving.

Her sister Tasha calls from Boise and says the cake has real butter and she's bringing her own. Tasha says 'unmedicated' as if it were a church she belongs to.

That night Lashonda eats a cold chicken thigh standing up and notices that it tastes good. She writes the date on the fourth pen with a Sharpie and puts it back on the butter shelf.
